title: Choosing Data Types Responsibly
learningObjectives: Recognize its syntax and important rules.
Explain the sample programs and predict their results.
Use this concept in a small program.
Identify common mistakes and choose a safer approach.

understand.concept: Choose a type based on the meaning, range, precision, and interfaces of the data. Use types that express intent and avoid overflow, loss of precision, or unnecessary conversions.
understand.whyItMatters: Correct data declarations and type choices make C++ programs easier to understand, safer and more portable.
understand.explain: Good type choices make program logic clearer and can prevent defects. Consider input limits, arithmetic behaviour, API requirements, and whether the value represents a quantity, measurement, status or text.

practise.guidedTask: Read each example for Choosing Data Types Responsibly. Predict what it does, compile locally if possible, change one value or declaration, then explain the difference.
practise.independentTask: Create a short C++ program using choosing data types responsibly in a practical context. Include at least three inputs or test cases, one boundary case, and a short explanation of your choices.

Use clear variable names and initialization.

questions.prompt: Which identifier is valid under the basic C++ naming rules?
questions.explanation: An identifier may contain digits after its first character and must not be a keyword.

questions.prompt: What is an initialization statement primarily doing?
options: Giving an object its starting value
questions.answer: Giving an object its starting value
questions.explanation: Initialization establishes an object's initial state.

questions.prompt: Why is brace initialization often recommended?
options: It helps reject many narrowing conversions
It automatically makes every value const
It guarantees zero runtime cost in every case
questions.answer: It helps reject many narrowing conversions
questions.explanation: List initialization diagnoses many narrowing conversions.

questions.prompt: Which type is generally suited to a true/false state?
What is the role of auto?
options: Compile-time type deduction from an initializer
Changing a variable's type at runtime
questions.answer: Compile-time type deduction from an initializer
questions.explanation: auto deduces a fixed type at compile time.

The object is always stored on disk
questions.answer: The object should not be modified through that name
questions.explanation: const restricts modification through a const-qualified object or reference.
sizeof yields the size of an object or type in bytes.

questions.prompt: Which is generally the best practice for choosing a type?
options: Match the value's meaning and range requirements
Always choose the smallest type regardless of interface
questions.answer: Match the value's meaning and range requirements
questions.explanation: Type selection should reflect semantics, range and interface requirements.

questions.prompt: Why avoid exact equality checks for computed floating-point values?
options: Binary floating-point values can have rounding representation differences
double cannot store any decimal values
Comparison operators are illegal on double
questions.answer: Binary floating-point values can have rounding representation differences
questions.explanation: Floating-point representation is approximate; tolerance-based comparison is often needed.

questions.prompt: Which type is typically a good default for general floating-point calculations?
questions.explanation: double is a practical default for general floating-point work.
